headline_en: Greek coast guard throwing migrants into the sea, eyewitnesses allege
summary_en: A BBC analysis reported that more than 40 migrants died in the Mediterranean over three years because of the Greek coast guard, at least nine of them after being thrown into the sea. The Greek coast guard denies the allegations. The piece concerns migrants in general (witnesses cited are from Cameroon); the only Bangladesh link is embedded related-story headlines.

facts.statement: The BBC verified 15 incidents between May 2020 and May 2023 in which 43 migrants died after being forced out of Greek waters or pushed back to sea after reaching Greek-controlled islands; witnesses say at least 9 of them were deliberately thrown into the sea by the Greek coast guard.
facts.source_in_article: BBC analysis (sources: local media, NGOs, Turkish coast guard)

facts.statement: According to witnesses interviewed by the BBC, in four incidents migrants who had already reached Greek islands were sent back, and in several incidents migrants were put on engineless dinghies and pushed out to sea towards Turkey.

A Cameroonian man said that in September 2021 he reached the coast of Samos island, Greece, planning to apply for political asylum; five masked police (two in black, three in plain clothes) seized him and two others (one Cameroonian, one Ivorian), put them on a coast guard boat and threw them into the sea; his two companions died and he was pushed towards Turkey without a life jacket.

The Greek coast guard denies the pushback allegations, saying its own inquiry found no truth in any allegation of illegal conduct. Greece has long been accused of forcibly pushing Europe-bound migrants back towards Turkey, which the article calls a clear violation of international law.

A related-story headline embedded in the article states that 21% of migrants entering Europe across the Mediterranean are Bangladeshi; another states that 2,500 migrants died or went missing in the Mediterranean 'this year' (no further detail given).

headline_en: 35 Bangladeshis adrift in the Mediterranean cling to rescuers on sight
summary_en: Before dawn on Monday 20 May 2024 the charity ship Ocean Viking rescued 35 Bangladeshis from a fibreglass boat in waters between Malta and Italy; they had been at sea three days after leaving Benghazi, Libya, bound for Sicily. The ship was sent to the Italian port of Ortona. Italy listed Bangladesh as a 'safe country' that month, making asylum harder.

facts.statement: 35 Bangladeshis were rescued before dawn on Monday 20 May 2024 from an overcrowded fibreglass boat in waters between Malta and Italy by the charity rescue ship Ocean Viking, operated by SOS Mediterranee. They said they had been on the boat three days, had travelled about 600 km from Benghazi, Libya, and were heading for Sicily, Italy.

Of the 35 rescued Bangladeshis, three needed urgent medical help and one was unconscious; they were wet, barefoot and shivering. Red Cross/Red Crescent staff gave water, food, blankets and black tracksuits.

The rescued Bangladeshis repeatedly asked the crew whether they were being sent back to Libya; IFRC operations manager Sara Mancinelli said they were assured they were safe and would not be returned to Libya, and that they were mentally devastated.

After rescue the 35 were registered and housed in a container on the ship's deck; an IFRC crew member explained what would happen next. Only one of the Bangladeshis knew English and translated for the others. The ship was assigned the Adriatic port of Ortona, Italy, more than two days' sailing away.
Under a policy introduced by Italy's far-right government, rescue ships may carry out one operation at a time and must then go straight to the assigned port.
In May 2024 Rome listed Bangladesh as a 'safe country', which means it will be hard for rescued Bangladeshis to seek asylum in Italy.

According to the UN's International Organization for Migration, 622 migrants died or went missing in the central Mediterranean from January 2024 to the time of the report; IOM confirms this route is the most dangerous for migrants.
SOS Mediterranee says it has rescued about 10,000 people from the Mediterranean with the Ocean Viking since 2019.

headline_en: Applications open for allowance for disabled children of expatriate workers
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board invited applications for its allowance for disabled children of migrant workers: BDT 1,000 a month for five years, effective 1 January 2024. Online applications opened 16 May 2024 and the deadline was 27 June 2024; the article lists eligibility, documents, the postal address and the Probashbondhu call centre numbers.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board (under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment) gives an allowance for disabled children of migrant workers: if selected, BDT 1,000 a month (BDT 12,000 a year) for a five-year term, effective from 1 January 2024.

Eligible for the disabled-child allowance: children of migrant workers who took BMET emigration clearance / Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, and, for deceased workers, those whose family received a financial grant from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board. The child's father, mother or guardian applies; a worker with more than one disabled child must apply separately for each.

Documents for the disabled-child allowance application: photocopy of the parent's passport; for a worker who died abroad, the NOC issued by the Bangladesh embassy; two attested passport-size photos of the child for a paper application or one photo for an online application; attested photocopy of the Suborno Nagorik (disability) ID card issued by the upazila social services office; photocopy of the parent's passport including the BMET emigration clearance page; and a bank account statement (with bank routing number) of the parent/guardian who will receive the cheque.

The allowance can be applied for online through the board's website (online applications began 16 May 2024) or in person/by post; deadline 27 June 2024. Those who had already applied did not need to apply again.

For a paper application the form is free from the Wage Earners' Welfare Board head office, the board's website, Welfare Centres or District Employment and Manpower Offices; the completed form with documents had to reach: Wage Earners' Welfare Board, 9th floor (Despatch section), Probashi Kallyan Bhaban, Eskaton Garden, Ramna, Dhaka by 27 June.
Probashbondhu Call Centre for any information: 16135 toll-free from inside Bangladesh, +8809610101030 from abroad.

headline_en: No report of any Bangladeshi student being badly injured in Kyrgyzstan: Foreign Minister
summary_en: After mob attacks on foreigners in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, that also hit Bangladeshi students, Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on 19 May 2024 that concern had been conveyed to the Kyrgyz government and no Bangladeshi student was reported badly hurt. Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the embassy in Uzbekistan covers it.

facts.statement: Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said on Sunday 19 May 2024 (at an OCAB event at the press club, Dhaka) that Bangladesh had conveyed concern to the Kyrgyz government over attacks on Bangladeshi students, that there was no report of any Bangladeshi student being badly injured, and that he had told the ambassador to go to Kyrgyzstan and observe the situation.

Attacks on foreigners began in Kyrgyzstan after a clash between some Egyptian medical students and some locals; Bangladeshi students in the capital Bishkek were also attacked. At least 800 Bangladeshi medical students were living in insecurity; videos showed students of various countries hiding 15-20 to a room, a man being beaten, and locals patrolling the city in convoys of 20-25 cars.

facts.statement: Bangladesh has no embassy in Kyrgyzstan; the Bangladesh embassy in Uzbekistan is responsible for Kyrgyzstan.
The Bangladesh embassy has no statistics on how many Bangladeshis are in Kyrgyzstan; it estimates 600 to 800 students and about a thousand workers.

headline_en: Cost of sending remittances from the UAE to rise
summary_en: Citing Gulf News, the article reports that UAE exchange houses will raise remittance fees by 15 percent (AED 2.5 per transaction) at their branches, probably from May 2024, the first rise in five years; digital and app transfers are not affected. The UAE is Bangladesh's largest remittance source.

facts.statement: Exchange houses in the UAE that belong to the Foreign Exchange and Remittance Group (FERG) agreed to raise the remittance fee by 15 percent, an increase of AED 2.5 per transaction, the first rise in five years. It applies only to transfers made at exchange-house branches; fees for online platforms and apps are not rising.
facts.source_in_article: Gulf News; Antony Jos, executive director of Joyalukkas Exchange

facts.statement: Under UAE consumer protection law, customers must be told at least two months before a fee increase.

Under the existing structure, sending remittance from the UAE to India or the Philippines costs AED 22 per transaction and to the UK AED 50, plus VAT. The fee to Pakistan equals India's but senders effectively pay nothing because the State Bank of Pakistan reimburses the fee. (The article does not give the fee to Bangladesh.)

Lulu Financial Holdings managing director Adeeb Ahamed said that even after the 15 percent rise the cost of remitting from the UAE is under 3.5 percent of the amount sent, against a global average of 6.2 percent.

Most people in the UAE still send money in person at exchange-house offices, which are usually near workers' factories and housing; few use digital channels. Exchange-house officials expect the fee rise to push workers towards cheaper digital transfers, as happened during Covid.

Remittances to Bangladesh from the UAE: about USD 2.07 billion in FY2021-22, about USD 3.03 billion in FY2022-23, and about USD 2.91 billion in the first eight months (July-February) of FY2023-24, when the UAE was the largest source, followed by the UK, Saudi Arabia, the USA and Italy.

headline_en: Wailing in the families of four workers kidnapped in Libya
summary_en: Four Bangladeshi masons from neighbouring villages of Lalmonirhat and Kurigram, working in Benghazi, Libya, were kidnapped on about 11 March 2024; callers demand ransom via bKash numbers in Bangladesh and threaten to kill them. The families accuse Libya-based fellow villagers, including the man through whom two of them migrated; the accused's father denies it. Two written complaints were filed at Lalmonirhat Sadar police station.

facts.statement: Four Bangladeshi workers who did masonry work in Benghazi, Libya, were kidnapped; families in Lalmonirhat and Kurigram were told by phone on 11 March 2024. They are Al Amin (23) of Sinduria village, Panchagram union, Lalmonirhat Sadar; his brother-in-law Hafizul Islam (40) of Ghorialdanga, Rajarhat, Kurigram; Al Amin (22) of Bhim Sharma village, Rajarhat; and his cousin Rakibul Islam (24) of Ramram village, Panchagram.

The kidnappers of Bangladeshi workers in Libya phone the families on imo and demand ransom be paid in instalments to bKash numbers held by the gang's members in Bangladesh, threatening to kill the captives and hide the bodies if not paid or if the family goes to the law.

Joynal Abedin said an unknown caller on his imo number at 8 am on 11 March 2024 demanded BDT 1 lakh ransom for his son Al Amin and son-in-law Hafizul, to be sent as BDT 50,000 each to two bKash numbers. Liton Mia, brother of the other Al Amin, said a caller from Libya at about 7:51 am the same day demanded BDT 5 lakh per person for the four. (The two demands differ.)

Joynal Abedin (60), a poor farmer of Sinduria village, Lalmonirhat, sold land and spent BDT 5 lakh three years earlier to send his only son Al Amin to Libya; the workers' families had borrowed, mortgaged or sold land to send them.

Families allege that Libya-based Mizanur Rahman (son of Abdul Monnaf, Sinduria village), through whom Al Amin and Hafizul went to Libya, is behind the kidnapping; Liton Mia also names Libya-based Md. Nazmul Huda (23, son of Samsul Haque, Ramram village) and Md. Sultan (32, son of Abu Bakkar Siddique, Ramram village). Mizanur's father Abdul Monnaf denies it, calling his son honest and the accusers jealous.

summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show USD 631.8 million in remittances through legal channels in the first nine days of February 2024, after USD 2.10 billion in January. The article repeats yearly totals for 2019-2023 and analysts' view that growth lags the number of workers going abroad.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 631.8 million (63 crore 18 lakh) through legal channels in the first nine days of February 2024: USD 69.1 million via state-owned banks, USD 29.6 million via one specialised bank, USD 531.6 million via private banks and USD 1.39 million via foreign banks.
Bangladesh received USD 2.10 billion in remittances in January 2024, the first month above USD 2 billion in six months.

Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.
Analysts say remittance growth is not meeting expectations because it is not rising in line with the number of workers sent abroad each year.

headline_en: Remittances cross USD 2 billion again, reserves fall
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 2.101 billion in remittances in January 2024, the highest in six months, while foreign reserves fell further. The article adds RMMRU figures: over 1.3 million workers went abroad in 2023, a record, up 13 percent, while remittances rose only 2.88 percent and female migration fell 27 percent.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 2,101.0 million in January 2024, the highest in six months (June 2023 had USD 2.19 billion); December 2023 brought USD 1,989.8 million and November 2023 USD 1.93 billion.

Bangladesh's gross foreign-exchange reserves were USD 25.09 billion on 31 January 2024 (USD 19.94 billion under IMF BPM6), down from USD 25.23 billion (BPM6 USD 20.02 billion) on 25 January, a fall of about USD 140 million in a week.

Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.

Because of the two-year foreign-currency crisis the official US dollar rate in Bangladesh rose from BDT 86 to BDT 110; banks were charging over BDT 120 per dollar for import payments because they were buying remittances at above the declared rate.

RMMRU told a press conference on Wednesday 31 January 2024 that more than 1.3 million (13 lakh) workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2023, the highest for any single year; overseas employment rose 13 percent over 2022 while remittances rose only 2.88 percent; male workers increased but female worker migration fell 27 percent from the previous year.

headline_en: Remittance growth only 3 percent in six months
summary_en: Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 21.90 billion in 2023, about 3 percent above 2022, despite record numbers of workers going abroad; July-December 2023 brought USD 10.80 billion, up about 2.75 percent. PRI's Ahsan H. Mansur blames continuing money laundering (hundi buyers purchasing expatriates' dollars abroad). The article gives the rates and incentives remitters receive.

facts.statement: Remittances received by Bangladesh by calendar year: USD 18.33 billion (1,833 crore) in 2019, USD 21.73 billion in 2020, USD 22.07 billion in 2021, USD 21.30 billion in 2022 and USD 21.90 billion in 2023, a growth of about 3 percent in 2023; 2023 was the second highest of the five years.

In the first six months of FY2023-24 (July-December 2023) remittances totalled USD 10.80 billion against USD 10.51 billion in the same period a year earlier, growth of about 2.75 percent. December 2023 brought USD 1.99 billion, the highest in six months (June 2023: USD 2.19 billion).
According to BMET, more than 1,210,000 workers went abroad in the 11 months to November 2023, against 1,136,000 in all of 2022; the higher outflow did not show up in remittances.
facts.source_in_article: Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET)

facts.statement: Expatriates sending money through legal channels were getting BDT 109.50 per US dollar (it was BDT 110.50 a month and a half earlier), plus a 2.5 percent government incentive and an equal incentive from the banks. BAFEDA and ABB set the dollar rate on the central bank's advice, but some banks were buying remittances at up to BDT 123.

The official dollar rate rose 5 percent during 2023 to BDT 110, while banks charged over BDT 120 for import payments because they bought remittances above the declared rate; some banks bought remittances at high prices and sold the dollars to the central bank, which is how the central bank was raising reserves.

Ahsan H. Mansur, executive director of the Policy Research Institute (PRI), said expatriates are sending money but legal remittances are not rising because money laundering continues: launderers buy expatriates' dollars abroad, and no action is taken against anyone.
A World Bank and KNOMAD report had projected Bangladesh's formal remittances at USD 23 billion for 2023; the actual figure was USD 21.90 billion.

headline_en: Coming from India, Myanmar, Taiwan, Pakistan, China and committing crimes in Bangladesh
summary_en: A long report on foreign nationals arrested for crimes inside Bangladesh (633 arrested between 5 August 2024 and September 2026, including for running scam centres). Its only material on Bangladeshis abroad: police say a foreign ring that took Bangladeshis to Cambodia and built scam centres there is now trying to set up scam centres in Bangladesh, and that many Bangladeshis are victims of Cambodia- and Myanmar-based scam centres after being trafficked with promises of high pay.

facts.statement: The article notes that scam centres based in Cambodia and Myanmar have recently been in the news for trafficking people abroad with a promise of high pay and then holding them hostage, and that many Bangladeshi citizens are among the victims.

Additional IGP (Crime and Operations) Md. Ahsan Habib Palash of Police Headquarters said a foreign ring had taken some Bangladeshis to Cambodia and built scam centres there, and with that ring's help is now trying to set up scam centres inside Bangladesh; law enforcement has them under surveillance.

facts.statement: On 11 September 2026 police arrested 70 foreign nationals from a building in Jalalabad residential area, Khulshi, Chattogram, for scam-centre-style online fraud and seized 170 electronic devices; on the night of 3 September 2026 six foreigners of a similar ring were arrested at a hotel in Cox's Bazar town. Those arrested in the two cases include nationals of China, Pakistan, Laos, Nepal, Vietnam and Taiwan who police say were trying to set up scam centres in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh law enforcement arrested 633 foreign nationals in about two years (5 August 2024 to September 2026): India 346, Myanmar 62, Taiwan 61, Laos 35, Pakistan 24, China 22, one each from Vietnam and Nepal, and 81 from Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and other countries; alleged crimes include online fraud, fake crypto or investment schemes, running scam centres, drug and gold smuggling, and human trafficking. 127 had been released on bail.

According to Special Branch (SB) and law-enforcement data, 2,268,065 foreigners entered Bangladesh in the 26 months from 5 August 2024 to September 2026, and 7,088 people from 126 countries were overstaying expired visas, most of them Indian (2,164) and Chinese (1,995).

Online tricks used by foreign-run rings in Bangladesh, per law enforcement: promises of quick big profits from investing in gold or bitcoin, befriending on social media and promising an expensive gift from abroad, and offers of attractive online earnings (e.g. an Amazon-lookalike site in August 2023 promising BDT 18,000 a month for 20 minutes' work a day; a Nigerian-led ring arrested July 2025 took BDT 18-20 lakh from over a hundred people).

headline_en: Execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia is a lesson for us: Shama Obaed
summary_en: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on 17 October 2026 that Saudi Arabia's execution of two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar, for an 'immoral act' inside a Makkah mosque is a big lesson, and urged expatriates to obey host-country laws. Bangladesh was not informed beforehand and has written to Saudi authorities for details; return of the bodies depends on the reply.

facts.statement: The Saudi Press Agency, citing the Saudi interior ministry, confirmed on Wednesday (about 14 October 2026) that two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar, were executed in Saudi Arabia. Gulf News reported they had been arrested by Saudi security forces for immoral and indecent acts inside a mosque in Makkah.

According to Gulf News, the two Bangladeshis were sentenced to death under 'ta'zir' (discretionary punishment by the judge under Sharia law), the judge citing violation of the sanctity of the mosque and the circumstances of the offence; a higher judicial authority upheld the verdict and a royal order directed that it be carried out.

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said the labour wing of the Bangladesh mission in Saudi Arabia reported that the two were engaged in 'adultery' inside a mosque in Makkah, a grave offence under Saudi law, but the Bangladesh government had received nothing officially and had written asking for details.
facts.source_in_article: Shama Obaed Islam, State Minister for Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Shama Obaed Islam advised Bangladeshis abroad to obey the law of whatever country they are in, saying Saudi Arabia has its own legal framework and anyone who commits a grave offence is punished under it; she called the two executions 'a big lesson for us'.

A source at the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah said Saudi authorities did not formally inform Bangladesh before the executions; the consulate learned from the media and on Friday 16 October 2026 wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry asking for details. The state minister said how the bodies can be brought back will be known once Saudi Arabia replies.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Consulate Jeddah source; Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial of the two Bangladeshis ran for several months in a Jeddah court and two prominent Bangladeshi citizens helped as interpreters. Unnamed foreign ministry officials said it was mysterious that no one contacted the mission on the detainees' behalf.
facts.source_in_article: unofficial sources; unnamed foreign ministry officials

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; under Article 36, when a foreign national is arrested the detaining state must, at the detainee's request, inform his country's consulate without delay and allow consular assistance. It was not clear whether the two executed Bangladeshis had asked for the consulate to be informed.

headline_en: Boat sinking on illegal voyage to Malaysia; Navy ship rescues passengers, 11 detained
summary_en: On the night of Thursday 1 October 2026 the Bangladesh Navy ship BNS Khalid Bin Walid rescued 76 people from a sinking wooden boat about 81 km west of the St Martin's Island lighthouse; 65 men, women and children were being trafficked to Malaysia. Eleven alleged traffickers on board were detained and are being handed to Teknaf police.

facts.statement: A wooden boat carrying 76 people for an illegal sea crossing to Malaysia via the Myanmar and Thailand coasts suffered engine failure deep in the Bay of Bengal, drifted and began taking on water about 81 km west of the St Martin's Island lighthouse (Teknaf, Cox's Bazar) in Bangladesh waters on the night of Thursday 1 October 2026.

According to the Navy, the 65 men, women and children on the boat had been either lured with promises of good jobs or kidnapped, held in remote areas of Teknaf, and then loaded on the boat by traffickers to be sent to Malaysia.

Alerted by fishermen, the Navy ship BNS Khalid Bin Walid rescued all 76, gave first aid, food and humanitarian help, and after screening detained 11 of them as traffickers; the boat was seized, and the 11 and the boat were being handed over to Teknaf police station for legal action.

The workers filed a formal complaint with Malaysia's labour department, Jabatan Tenaga Kerja (JTK).

facts.statement: All workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing (1969) Sdn Bhd, a Malaysian maker of bedding products employing Bangladeshis, had received no wages for three months as of June 2026; they cannot meet daily costs or send money home, and many who borrowed at high interest to migrate cannot pay instalments.

facts.statement: About 35 workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing have no valid visa or work permit (PLKS): they entered Malaysia legally but the company did not renew their work permits on time, leaving them in fear of arrest or fines.

Workers at Aerofoam Manufacturing allege they are forced to work overtime against their will without adequate rest, get no transport to the workplace, and the company has no effective grievance mechanism.

The affected Bangladeshi workers submitted a formal written complaint to 'Jabatan Tenaga Kerja' (JTK), the labour department of Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources, demanding prompt payment of arrears, regularisation of visas and work permits for the 35, return of passports, an end to forced overtime, a safe workplace, and investigation of high recruitment fees and irregularities in the migration process; they also asked that the company not retaliate.

headline_en: Malaysia dream lost in the waves of the Andaman Sea
summary_en: A Malaysia-bound trawler from the Teknaf coast carrying at least 250 Bangladeshis and Rohingya sank in the Andaman Sea on 8 April 2026; only nine were rescued, and the six Bangladeshi survivors were charged under the human trafficking law and jailed. Seven young men from three villages of Rajakhali union, Pekua, who left Teknaf by trawler on 4 April have been out of contact since 8 April. facts.statement: A Malaysia-bound trawler that left the Teknaf coast of Cox's Bazar sank in the Andaman Sea on the morning of 8 April 2026 because of strong wind, rough sea and overloading; at least 250 Bangladeshi and Rohingya men and women were on board. The Coast Guard said no trace of the missing or wreckage had been found.

At midday on 9 April 2026 the Bangladesh-flagged merchant ship 'Meghna Pride' rescued eight men and one woman found floating with water drums and pieces of wood near the Andaman Islands; they were handed that night to the Coast Guard ship Mansur Ali and then to Teknaf police station.

Mohiuddin Hridoy, 42, of Mirsarai, Chattogram) were charged under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act and sent to jail, with 10-15 unnamed accused also in the case.

Brokers target unemployed, indebted young men of poor families and offer to take them to Malaysia by boat for free, saying payment can be made after arrival in Malaysia, and promise very high-paying jobs. facts.statement: The body of S M Tarek, a Bangladeshi killed in Bahrain in the Middle East war, was flown from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on a Gulf Air flight to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on Friday 3 April 2026 and received by Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, State Minister Nurul Haque and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the Wage Earners' Welfare Board gave the dead worker's family BDT 35,000 for burial and BDT 50,000 immediately, and that BDT 3 lakh in financial assistance and BDT 10 lakh in insurance would also be paid; he promised long-term support in coordination with the local MP.
facts.source_in_article: Ariful Haque Chowdhury, Expatriates' Welfare Minister

facts.statement: Six Bangladeshis had died in the Middle East war as of 3 April 2026, according to the Expatriates' Welfare Minister; State Minister Nurul Haque said the bodies of three had reached Bangladesh so far.

The Expatriates' Welfare, Foreign Affairs, and Civil Aviation and Tourism ministries are coordinating with families and the countries concerned to speed up repatriation of bodies of Bangladeshis killed in the Middle East war; the ministry says it keeps constant contact with each family.

The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry says it continues to issue instructions and awareness messages asking Bangladeshis in the Middle East to stay on maximum alert; the government is making diplomatic efforts to get expatriates' visa validity extended in the war situation.

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said quick steps were being taken to bring home Bangladeshis held in camps in Greece, and that the government is taking a hard line to bring human traffickers to justice.

headline_en: Came abroad for a living, now helpless in the middle of a war
summary_en: A Middle East Eye feature on migrant workers in the Gulf during the war that followed the US-Israeli strike on Iran on 28 February 2026: delivery riders paid per delivery keep working under missile attack, every civilian killed in the UAE so far was a Bangladeshi, Nepali or Pakistani worker, and rights group Equidem says workers are left out of official safety guidance. Bahrain arrested five Pakistanis and one Bangladeshi for praising the attacks while filming, and filming security incidents carries prison risk in the UAE.

facts.statement: Since the war began after the US-Israeli strike on Iran on 28 February 2026, at least 12 civilians have been killed in Iranian attacks on Gulf countries; every civilian killed in the UAE so far was a migrant worker from Bangladesh, Nepal or Pakistan. One was Bangladeshi Saleh Ahmed (55), killed on the first day of the war while delivering water in the UAE.

Equidem executive director Mustafa Qadri said its researcher network in the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Jordan documented that migrant workers are effectively excluded from government safety communication: although some official statements mention 'all residents', workers say they got no workable guidance on shelters, safe evacuation routes or emergency help.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafa Qadri, Equidem, to Middle East Eye

facts.statement: Delivery riders in the UAE are paid only per delivery, so they have no income if they do not go out; a Pakistani rider in Dubai works 12-hour shifts and lives in a shared mess. Three riders on major UAE delivery platforms said they work at risk of death with no guidance, support or alternative, and workload multiplied after the war began as residents stayed indoors.
facts.source_in_article: delivery riders quoted by Middle East Eye

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi rider with two years at one company in Dubai said streets were empty on the day of the first attack but he had to go back out delivering the next day; customers were tipping somewhat more than usual.
Earlier in the week before 16 March 2026 Bahrain arrested five Pakistani and one Bangladeshi worker, accused of praising Iran's attack while filming its aftermath.

Mustafa Qadri warned that more workers may be arrested and face harsh administrative action for filming attack scenes, with the risk highest in the UAE, which has a record of jailing people for filming security-related incidents.

Qadri said labour-sending countries such as Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Kenya and Ethiopia have a historically weak record of meaningful diplomatic support for their citizens, and their response so far has been very inadequate; Western states under pressure to evacuate their own nationals put little pressure on Gulf states over migrant workers' safety.

Shaheen Abdullah, a shop owner in Doha, Qatar, said a burning splinter fell in front of his car during an explosion near his home, and that shops, restaurants and delivery services cannot close: 'no one can take even one day off'; evacuation, as European countries arrange for their citizens, is not something migrants with nothing to return to can consider.

Nepali workers are preferred for jobs on US and Western military bases in the Gulf because of Nepal's 'neutral' position; when risk rises Western civilians are evacuated but migrant workers are kept on to run cooking and cleaning services.

headline_en: Government will arrange quick travel for expatriates once flights resume
summary_en: After Iranian counter-attacks on Middle East countries killed two Bangladeshis and injured seven in two days, the foreign ministry held an inter-ministerial meeting on Monday 2 March 2026. The government promised to arrange travel for Middle East-bound passengers as soon as flights resume, set up a visa cell for those whose visas will expire, and said bodies will be brought home when conditions allow.

facts.statement: A foreign ministry notice said two Bangladeshis were killed and seven injured in missile and drone attacks in various Middle East countries over two days. In the UAE, Saleh Ahmed of Barlekha, Sylhet, died under rubble after an air strike on a civilian facility; in Bahrain one Bangladeshi was killed and three injured.

Four Bangladeshis were injured in a drone attack near the civilian airport in Kuwait: Aminul Islam of Nabinagar, Brahmanbaria; Rabiul Islam of Santhia, Pabna; Masudur Rahman of Begumganj, Noakhali; and Dulal Mia of Chandina, Cumilla.

At the inter-ministerial meeting chaired by Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman on 2 March 2026, the government promised that once the situation normalises and flights resume it will arrange travel for Middle East-bound passengers in the shortest possible time; flights were suspended and some workers were stuck in Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: government, inter-ministerial meeting; adviser Humayun Kabir

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said a cell has been formed on visa matters and that those whose visas will expire (because they cannot travel) will be helped through contact with the embassies concerned.

The Bangladesh embassy in the UAE is in contact with local authorities over Saleh Ahmed's death and his body will be repatriated once commercial flights resume; State Minister Shama Obaed Islam said families of the dead had been contacted and the government will bring the bodies when the situation normalises. The mission in Manama is in contact with Bahraini authorities.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs notice; Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: On 2 March 2026 the foreign ministers of Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE and Qatar's state minister for foreign affairs each phoned Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman about the crisis and the safety of Bangladeshi migrants; the Kuwait, Bahrain and UAE ministers expressed condolences and reaffirmed protection of civilians. Khalilur Rahman said the safety of Bangladeshis in the region is Bangladesh's priority and called for a diplomatic solution.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs; Khalilur Rahman

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Shipping Corporation ship 'Banglar Joyjatra' was stuck at Jebel Ali port, UAE; the embassy was in close contact with the captain and all crew were safe.

headline_en: 'Your son is no more, recite Inna Lillah'
summary_en: Md. Fahad (18), a class-ten student from Chandanaish, Chattogram, was sent to South Africa through brokers for BDT 9 lakh. He flew from Dhaka on 30 January 2026 to Ethiopia, but instead of a second flight was taken overland through jungle for about two weeks, robbed on the way, and died the night he reached Musina, South Africa, on 15 February 2026.

facts.statement: Brokers promised to fly Md. Fahad from Dhaka to Ethiopia and then to Zimbabwe and take him across the border into South Africa; in reality, after the 30 January 2026 flight from Dhaka to Ethiopia he was moved overland through several countries, walking through jungle at times (about 15 days), to Zimbabwe and then by road to Musina, South Africa, arriving Sunday 15 February 2026.

Nur Mohammad paid the broker ring BDT 2 lakh first and BDT 7 lakh more through a bank account number when the journey began (BDT 9 lakh, all borrowed from various people); a further BDT 1.5 lakh was due after arrival in South Africa. After Fahad's death the brokers promised to refund the money.

Md. Fahad (18), of North Joara village, Joara union, Chandanaish, Chattogram, died on the night of 15 February 2026 in Musina, South Africa, hours after arriving and resting in a room; the family believes the long journey, starvation, illness and lack of treatment killed him. A stranger who found the address in his passport and papers phoned his father.

headline_en: Expatriate kidnapped in Libya and ransom extracted; youth arrested in Sylhet
summary_en: RAB arrested Sadek Ahmed (30) at Beanibazar, Sylhet, on Monday 19 January 2026 over the kidnapping for ransom in Libya of Sumon Mia of Sonargaon, Narayanganj. Sumon had given his expired passport to an acquaintance, Abu Bakkar, for renewal; in September 2025 he was kidnapped and his family sent BDT 317,000 to three bKash numbers, after which contact was lost.

facts.statement: Sumon Mia, in Libya for eight years, gave his passport to an acquaintance there, Abu Bakkar, to get its validity extended after it expired in June 2025; on 13 September 2025 he phoned his family saying Abu Bakkar and 3-4 unknown people had kidnapped him and were demanding money under threat of death.

RAB arrested Sadek Ahmed (30) of Khashir village, Beanibazar, Sylhet, on the night of Monday 19 January 2026; he was handed to Jalalabad police on 20 January and sent to jail through court. RAB-9 Additional SP K M Shahidul Islam said steps to arrest the others were in process.

headline_en: Why should migration begin with debt and despair
summary_en: An op-ed by the ILO country director and IOM chief of mission in Bangladesh argues that recruitment cost is the biggest barrier to safe migration. It cites an average migration cost above USD 3,500 (about 10 months' earnings), Bangladeshis paying two to three times what Indians or Nepalis pay for the same jobs in the GCC and Malaysia, and calls for tighter control of recruiters and accountability for excess fees.

facts.statement: According to the Labour Force Survey 2024, the average cost of migration for a Bangladeshi worker is over USD 3,500 (BDT 462,000), which takes about 10 months of work to earn back.
facts.source_in_article: Labour Force Survey 2024, cited by ILO and IOM heads

facts.statement: In the GCC countries and Malaysia, Bangladeshi workers pay two to three times more than Indian or Nepali workers for the same job, a gap the authors say is well known to foreign employers and governments.

A worker named Shafiqul borrowed about USD 5,000 (over BDT 5 lakh), the price demanded by village brokers, to secure an ordinary construction job in Saudi Arabia the previous year; earning BDT 30,000-40,000 a month, he spent almost his entire first year repaying the loan.
BDT 30,000 to 40,000 a month is described as close to the average wage of low-skilled Bangladeshi migrant workers.
More than 13 million (1 crore 30 lakh) Bangladeshi workers are working in the Gulf, South-East Asia and elsewhere; in 2024 they sent home an estimated USD 26.9 billion, about 6 percent of GDP.

The authors say heavy migration debt forces workers to accept low wages, unsafe conditions and excess hours, limits their ability to bargain or complain, and leads to disputes, frequent changes of employer, overstaying and irregular work; they call for strict control of recruiters, an effective complaints system and clear liability for excess fees, noting the Labour Reform Commission has prioritised recruitment fees.

As human-rights and due-diligence laws tighten in major markets, companies are held accountable for fair recruitment too; since reimbursing excess fees is costly, employers are becoming more interested in hiring from countries with transparent, regulated recruitment systems.

headline_en: 15 injured in attack by rivals over human trafficking case in Madaripur
summary_en: At least 15 people were injured on the night of Friday 21 November 2025 in Purba Botla, Dasar upazila, Madaripur, in an attack that victims say was led by local broker Nasir Howlader against witnesses in a human trafficking case. The case was filed after Siam Howlader went missing two years earlier on the Libya route to Italy. Nasir denies it and police attribute the clash to a land dispute.

facts.statement: Siam Howlader, son of Habib Howlader of Purba Botla, Baligram union, Dasar, Madaripur, left home two years earlier to go to Italy by an illegal route with the help of local broker Nasir Howlader; he went missing on the way to Italy via Libya and has not been traced.
Siam Howlader's family filed a case under the human trafficking law against Nasir Howlader and five others (six accused) over his disappearance on the Libya-Italy route.

Injured witness Sabuj Howlader said that after a milad at Salam Howlader's house on Friday 21 November 2025, over a hundred people led by Nasir, with Rafiq, Salam and others, attacked Siam's relatives, who are witnesses in the trafficking case, with sticks and local weapons, vandalised and looted homes and threatened to kill them before going to jail. At least 15 were hurt and 11 seriously injured were admitted to Madaripur 250-bed Hospital. (The article's list of injured also includes a Nasir Howlader, 33.)

Nasir Howlader denied involvement, calling the trafficking case false. Dasar police OC Sheikh Md. Ehteshamul Islam said the attack arose from a land dispute within the Howlader clan, that neither side had filed a complaint, and police would act if one was filed.
